a: a second time, just as he had appeared to him at Gibeon
p: God speaks to Solomon in a vision twice: once at the start of his reign and once at its height.
b: The first appearance came in a dream at Gibeon, where the young king asked for a listening heart (3:4–15). That vision was all promise. This one, after twenty years of building, is mostly warning. The narrator will remember both visits when Solomon falls: the LORD "had shown himself to him two times" (11:9). A king who had heard God twice had less excuse than anyone. 2 Chronicles 7:12–22 gives a fuller version of this speech, adding the famous promise that if God's people humble themselves and pray, he will hear and heal their land (2 Chronicles 7:14).

a: My eyes and my heart will be there
p: God answers Solomon's prayer in its own words: his eyes will be on the house.
b: In his prayer Solomon asked God to "keep your eyes open toward this house" night and day (8:29). God gives more than he was asked: his eyes and his heart. The heart in Hebrew is the seat of thought and will, not only of feeling, so the promise means God's attention and purpose rest on the temple. Yet the same speech goes on to warn that God can throw this house "out of my sight" (9:7). The temple is a gift, not a guarantee.

a: honest in heart and upright
p: Hebrew: 'in wholeness of heart and in uprightness.' David's adultery and murder are not forgotten.
b: The word tom means completeness or integrity, from the same root as tamim, "blameless." It describes a heart that is not divided, not a life without sin. Kings holds up David as the standard for every king of Judah (11:4, 6; 15:3, 11), and it does so knowing about Bathsheba and Uriah: one later verse even names "the affair of Uriah the Hittite" as the exception (15:5). What sets David apart in Kings is that he never worshiped other gods. His heart stayed with the LORD even when his life went wrong.
orig: בְתָם־לֵבָב וּבְיֹשֶׁר (betom-levav uveyosher), 'in wholeness of heart and in uprightness'

a: A man of yours will never be cut off from Israel's throne
p: Nathan's promise to David sounded unconditional. Here it comes with an 'if.' Readers have long asked how the two fit.
b: In 2 Samuel 7 God tells David, "Your throne will stand firm for all time" (2 Samuel 7:16), with no condition attached, though the son who does wrong will be corrected "with a rod" (2 Samuel 7:14). Here (and in 2:4; 8:25) the promise depends on obedience. Many critical scholars see two layers: an older unconditional royal promise, and a later exilic edition that explains why the dynasty fell. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers answer that the promise of the line itself never failed, while each king's enjoyment of it depended on faithfulness. Christians see the line kept alive in Jesus, the son of David (Matthew 1:1). Note that the condition here is about "the throne of Israel," and Solomon's son keeps only Judah.

a: an example in people's sayings and a target of their jokes
p: The words come from Moses' list of covenant curses.
b: Deuteronomy warns that a disobedient Israel will become "an example in their sayings and a target of their jokes, among all the peoples the LORD drives you to" (Deuteronomy 28:37). The two Hebrew words here, mashal (a saying or proverb) and sheninah (a sharp jibe), are the same pair. Kings is written in Deuteronomy's language from start to finish, and this speech points ahead to the end of the story: the temple burned and the people exiled (2 Kings 25). Jeremiah repeats the warning almost word for word (Jeremiah 24:9).

a: will be stunned and will whistle
p: To whistle at a ruin was a gesture of shock, a little like a long, low 'whew.'
b: The verb sharaq means to hiss or whistle. Passersby whistle at ruined cities in Jeremiah, Lamentations and Zephaniah (Jeremiah 19:8; Lamentations 2:15–16; Zephaniah 2:15). It may have been a way of warding off the bad luck clinging to a cursed place, or simply a sound of amazement. Either way, the grand building that people now come to admire will one day be the thing they whistle at.

a: And the answer will be
t: A question and answer about ruins
p: Ancient texts explain a disaster by asking 'Why?' and answering 'Because they broke the covenant.'
b: The same pattern appears in Deuteronomy: "Every nation will ask, 'Why did the LORD treat this land this way?' ... And the answer will be: 'They walked away from the covenant of the LORD'" (Deuteronomy 29:24–25), and again in Jeremiah 22:8–9. Moshe Weinfeld pointed out a close parallel in the annals of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal (7th century BC), where people of Arabia ask why disaster has struck them and answer that they broke their oaths to the great god of Assyria. Covenant language was the shared diplomatic language of the age.

a: King Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in the land of Galilee
p: Kings has Solomon hand over towns to pay his bills. Chronicles has Hiram give towns to Solomon.
b: According to Kings, Solomon paid for the timber and gold with land in western Galilee, on the border with Tyre. 2 Chronicles 8:2 tells it the other way: "the towns that Huram had given to Solomon, Solomon rebuilt, and settled Israelites there" (fresh rendering). Some harmonize: Hiram refused the towns (9:12–13) and gave them back. Many critical scholars think Chronicles quietly changed a story that made Solomon look like a debtor who gave away part of the promised land. Either way, 9:14 suggests Hiram also lent or paid Solomon a large sum of gold.

a: the land of Cabul
p: The name sounds like Hebrew for 'like nothing.' Josephus says it meant 'not pleasing' in Phoenician.
b: Hebrew readers heard ke-bal, "like nothing": Hiram calls the towns worthless. Josephus explains the name as a Phoenician word meaning "not pleasing" (Antiquities 8.142), which fits 9:12. There was a real town named Cabul in the territory of Asher (Joshua 19:27), still called Kabul today, so the story may be a play on an existing name. "My brother" is the language of treaties between equal kings, used again in 20:32–33.

a: the forced labor King Solomon raised
p: This chapter says Solomon enslaved only the Canaanites (9:20–22). Chapter 5 says he drafted 'all Israel.'
b: The word mas means a labor draft. In 5:13–14 Solomon raises a mas "from all Israel," thirty thousand men working in shifts. Here, the permanent slave labor (mas 'oved, 9:21) falls only on the surviving Canaanites, while Israelites serve as soldiers and officers (9:22). One reading sees two kinds of service: Israelites did temporary shifts, Canaanites lifelong labor. Another sees an editor softening the memory of Solomon. The complaint at Shechem (12:4) and the stoning of the labor chief (12:18) show that the northern tribes, at least, felt the yoke.

a: Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer
p: Three cities with nearly identical six-chambered gates became a famous test case for archaeology.
b: In the 1950s Yigael Yadin noticed that the city gates of Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer had the same plan: six chambers, three on each side of the passage. He took this verse as the key and called them "Solomonic gates." For decades this was a textbook example of the Bible and the spade agreeing. Since the 1990s Israel Finkelstein and others have argued, mainly on pottery and radiocarbon dating, that the gates belong to the 9th century, the time of Omri and Ahab. Amihai Mazar, William Dever and others still defend a 10th-century date, at least for Gezer and Hazor. The debate is unsettled; see the topic page.

a: Then he gave it as a parting gift to his daughter, Solomon's wife
p: Egyptian kings rarely gave their daughters to foreign kings. Which pharaoh this was is unknown.
b: The Hebrew shilluchim is a gift that goes with a bride when she leaves home. An Egyptian princess married to a king of Israel was remarkable: in the 14th century BC Pharaoh Amenhotep III wrote to a Babylonian king that "from of old, a king's daughter of Egypt has not been given to anyone" (Amarna letter EA 4). Egypt was weaker in Solomon's century. K. A. Kitchen and others suggest Pharaoh Siamun, who has left a relief of himself smiting an enemy, possibly a Philistine; others think the story reflects later times. No Egyptian record names the marriage.

a: the Israelites had not been able to put them under the ban
p: Joshua and Judges said some Canaanites were never driven out. Solomon makes them a labor force.
b: "Under the ban" (cherem) means devoted to God by total destruction (Deuteronomy 7:2; 20:17). The books before Kings admit the conquest was incomplete and that Israel put the remaining Canaanites to forced labor instead (Joshua 16:10; 17:13; Judges 1:28–35). Here that compromise becomes state policy. The list of five peoples echoes the standard list of the land's former nations (Deuteronomy 7:1).

a: five hundred and fifty of them
p: Chronicles counts 250 chief officers. Added to the other lists, both books reach the same total.
b: 2 Chronicles 8:10 gives 250. In 5:16 Kings counts 3,300 foremen, and 2 Chronicles 2:18 counts 3,600. The totals match: 3,300 + 550 = 3,850, and 3,600 + 250 = 3,850. Many commentators, ancient and modern, think the two books divide the same body of officers differently, perhaps between Israelite and Canaanite overseers. It is a good example of how a difference that looks like a contradiction can come from two ways of grouping one number.
orig: חֲמִשִּׁים וַחֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת (chamishim vachamesh me'ot), 'fifty and five hundred'

a: Three times a year
p: The king led worship at the three great feasts the law required.
b: The law commanded every Israelite male to appear before the LORD "three times a year": at Unleavened Bread, Weeks and Booths (Exodus 23:14–17; Deuteronomy 16:16). Solomon offers on those occasions, as a king who also acts as chief worshiper. The incense he burns may mean he served at the incense altar inside the temple, a role later limited to priests (2 Chronicles 26:16–18). The Greek translation does not have 9:15–25 here; most of it appears at other places in its account of Solomon, one of several signs that the Greek and Hebrew editions of these chapters were arranged differently.

a: the Sea of Reeds
t: The Sea of Reeds at Eloth
p: Here the 'Sea of Reeds' (Yam Suf) is clearly the Gulf of Aqaba, the eastern arm of the Red Sea.
b: This site renders yam suf as "Sea of Reeds" everywhere, including in the exodus story (Exodus 13:18; 15:4). In this verse the name plainly means the Gulf of Aqaba, since Eloth (Elath, near modern Eilat and Aqaba) lies on its shore. That shows the Hebrew name could cover the arms of the Red Sea, which matters for the debate over where Israel crossed. Nelson Glueck identified Ezion-geber with Tell el-Kheleifeh near Aqaba; later study of his finds dated that site mostly after Solomon, and the port's location is still uncertain.

a: They reached Ophir
p: Ophir's gold was famous, but no one knows for sure where Ophir was: Arabia, East Africa and India are all suggested.
b: "Gold of Ophir" became a byword for the finest gold (Job 22:24; Psalm 45:9; Isaiah 13:12). A pottery fragment found at Tell Qasile, near Tel Aviv, from about the 8th century BC, reads "gold of Ophir to Beth-horon, thirty shekels," which shows the name was a real trade term. Genesis 10:29 lists Ophir among the Arabian peoples, which points to southern or western Arabia. Others suggest the Horn of Africa, the Egyptians' land of Punt. Josephus placed it in India (Antiquities 8.164). The three-year voyages of 10:22 suggest a long way. Chronicles has 450 talents instead of 420 (2 Chronicles 8:18), and the Greek has 120; see the variant.

a: The queen of Sheba
p: Most scholars place Sheba in Yemen, home of the Sabaean kingdom; Ethiopian tradition places her across the Red Sea.
b: Sheba (Hebrew Sheva) is best known as Saba, the kingdom of the Sabaeans in what is now Yemen, with its capital at Marib and its great dam. Its wealth came from frankincense and myrrh carried north by camel to Gaza and Damascus. Genesis also lists a Sheba among the Arabian peoples near Dedan in the north (Genesis 10:28; Genesis 25:3), and Assyrian records of the 8th century name Sabaean chiefs and several Arabian queens. Sabaean inscriptions so far name no queen, and the kingdom is not well documented before about 800 BC, so some historians doubt a 10th-century queen. Others answer that the trade route itself is old. Ethiopia's tradition makes her queen of Aksum; see the topic page.
r: Genesis 10:7; Genesis 10:28; Genesis 25:3; Job 6:19; Psalm 72:10; Isaiah 60:6; Ezekiel 27:22

a: news tied to the name of the LORD
t: Solomon's fame and the LORD's name
p: The Hebrew is terse: 'the report of Solomon, to the name of the LORD.' Its sense is debated.
b: Some take it as "his fame because of the LORD's name," that is, the fame of the temple he built for the LORD's name (8:20). Others read "his fame, which brought honor to the LORD's name." Some critics suspect a later addition, since the parallel in 2 Chronicles 9:1 lacks the phrase. Whatever the grammar, the effect is the same: the foreign queen's visit is tied to Israel's God, and she ends by blessing him (10:9).
orig: שֵׁמַע שְׁלֹמֹה לְשֵׁם יְהוָה (shema Shelomoh leshem YHWH)

a: to put him to the test with riddles
p: Hebrew chidot are riddles and puzzling sayings, the stuff of wisdom contests.
b: A chidah is the word for Samson's riddle (Judges 14:12–19) and for the dark sayings of the wise (Proverbs 1:6; Psalm 49:4). Royal courts in the ancient Near East enjoyed contests of wit. Later Jewish writers filled in the riddles: the Targum Sheni to Esther and the Midrash on Proverbs give a set of them, such as a test to tell boys from girls dressed alike, or real flowers from artificial ones. Josephus adds that Hiram and Solomon had swapped riddles too (Antiquities 8.143).

a: camels loaded with spices
p: Camel caravans from southern Arabia carried frankincense and myrrh to the Mediterranean.
b: The Hebrew besamim means fragrant spices and resins, above all frankincense and myrrh, which grew in southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa. Caravans traveled some 1,500 miles north along the edge of the desert. Camels were domesticated as pack animals in the region in the late second and early first millennium BC; finds at Timna in the Arabah show their use in the copper trade by the 10th century. A trade mission dressed as a royal visit fits what we know: trade between kings was often carried on as an exchange of gifts.

a: the burnt offerings he offered up at the LORD's house
p: The Hebrew 'olato means 'his burnt offering.' Chronicles reads a near word meaning 'his upper room' or 'ascent.'
b: The parallel in 2 Chronicles 9:4 has 'aliyyato, "his upper room" or "his ascent," probably a private stairway or passage from the palace up to the temple (compare 2 Kings 16:18). The KJV follows that sense here: "his ascent by which he went up." The two words share the root "go up." The Plain English Translation follows the plain Hebrew of Kings, which makes the queen's last impression a worship scene.
orig: וְעֹלָתוֹ אֲשֶׁר יַעֲלֶה (ve'olato asher ya'aleh), 'and his burnt offering that he offered up'

a: It left her breathless
p: Literally, 'there was no more breath (ruach) in her.'
b: The same phrase is used of the kings of Canaan who lost heart when Israel crossed the Jordan (Joshua 5:1) and of Rahab's people (Joshua 2:11, with a near phrase). It means to be overwhelmed, whether by fear or by wonder. A queen who came to test Solomon goes home without her breath.
orig: וְלֹא־הָיָה בָהּ עוֹד רוּחַ (velo-hayah vah od ruach)

a: The LORD's love for Israel lasts forever
p: The queen praises the LORD and names the king's purpose: justice and right.
b: Her blessing echoes Hiram's (5:7) and fulfills Solomon's prayer that foreigners would come because of God's name (8:41–43). Her words also define kingship. A king exists "to do what is just and right" (mishpat utsedaqah), the pair used of David (2 Samuel 8:15) and of the ideal king in Psalm 72, a psalm titled "For Solomon" that pictures "the kings of Sheba and Seba" bringing gifts (Psalm 72:10). Isaiah 60:6 sees nations coming from Sheba with gold and frankincense, which Christian readers connect with the Magi (Matthew 2:11).
r: 5:7; 8:41–43; 2 Samuel 8:15; Psalm 72:1–2; Psalm 72:10; Isaiah 60:6; Jeremiah 22:15; Matthew 2:11

a: almug wood
p: No one knows what almug wood was. Guesses include red sandalwood and a kind of juniper.
b: Chronicles spells it algummim and says it came from Lebanon (2 Chronicles 2:8; 2 Chronicles 9:10–11). A word almg appears in texts from Ugarit and Alalakh as a valuable wood, which suggests a tree of Syria or Anatolia. Because this verse has it arriving from Ophir, older commentators guessed red sandalwood from India. The Greek translators did not know either and wrote "hewn wood."

a: Whatever the queen of Sheba wanted and asked for
p: Ethiopian tradition says the queen bore Solomon a son, Menelik, the first king of Ethiopia.
b: The Hebrew says Solomon gave her "all her desire," a phrase that later readers took more than one way. The Ethiopian national epic, the Kebra Nagast ("Glory of the Kings," written down in the 14th century from older traditions), names the queen Makeda and tells how Solomon fathered her son Menelik, who later brought the ark of the covenant to Aksum. Ethiopia's emperors claimed descent from them until 1974. Jewish legend tells a different and sometimes hostile story; Islamic tradition names her Bilqis (see the topic page). The biblical text says nothing of a child, and most historians treat these as later national and religious traditions.

a: gold weighing six hundred and sixty-six talents
p: About 25 tons of gold a year. The number reappears in Revelation as the number of the beast.
b: A talent was roughly 30–34 kilograms (66–75 pounds), so 666 talents is some 20–25 tons, a figure most historians treat as royal splendor rather than accounts. Outside this verse and its copy in 2 Chronicles 9:13, the number 666 occurs only in Ezra 2:13 (a family count) and Revelation 13:18. A few interpreters, ancient and modern, suggest that John's "666" deliberately recalls Solomon's gold, a king corrupted by wealth; most read it as the numerical value of a name, probably Nero. The link is possible but not proven.

a: two hundred body-length shields made of hammered gold
p: Shields for show, not war. Shishak will carry them off, and Rehoboam will replace them with bronze (14:26–27).
b: The tsinnah was a large shield covering the whole body; the magen (10:17) was a smaller round one. Gold is too soft for battle, so these were ceremonial, carried by the royal guard on state occasions (14:28). Six hundred shekels is about 7 kilograms (15 pounds) of gold each. A mina was 50 or 60 shekels (Ezekiel 45:12), so the smaller shields used 150–180 shekels; 2 Chronicles 9:16 says "three hundred," without naming the unit. The House of the Forest of Lebanon, the great cedar hall of 7:2–5, served partly as an armory (Isaiah 22:8).

a: two lions stood beside the arms
p: Lions beside a throne were a royal symbol across the ancient Near East.
b: Thrones flanked by lions or winged lion-sphinxes are known from Egypt, Syria and Assyria; an ivory plaque from Megiddo shows a Canaanite king on a throne with winged lions. Ivory was carved panels set into a wooden frame, not solid tusk; carved ivories from 9th-century Samaria show the style (22:39; Amos 6:4). The lion was also Judah's emblem (Genesis 49:9). Later Jewish legend turned Solomon's throne into a marvel of moving lions and eagles (Targum Sheni to Esther 1:2).

a: Tarshish ships
p: A kind of large ship for long voyages, named after a far western port, not a ship that actually went to Tarshish.
b: Tarshish was a distant port in the west, often identified with Tartessos in southern Spain (Jonah 1:3), though some suggest Sardinia or Tarsus. "Tarshish ships" became a name for big seagoing merchant ships, as "East Indiaman" did in English. These sailed from the Red Sea (22:48), so they were not going to Spain. Chronicles took the phrase literally: "ships going to Tarshish" (2 Chronicles 9:21; 2 Chronicles 20:36). The Greek translators read "ships of Tharsis."
r: 22:48; 2 Chronicles 9:21; 2 Chronicles 20:36; Psalm 48:7; Isaiah 2:16; Isaiah 23:1; Jonah 1:3

a: monkeys and apes
p: The two animal words are rare loanwords. The KJV's 'peacocks' is one old guess; 'baboons' or 'monkeys' is another.
b: Qof is related to Egyptian gif and Sanskrit kapi, "monkey." Tukki was once linked to a Tamil word for peacock (tokai), which gave the KJV "apes, and peacocks" and supported an Indian Ophir. Many scholars now prefer an Egyptian word ky, a kind of monkey or baboon, which fits a route along the African coast. The Plain English Translation gives two kinds of monkey, which is the likeliest sense. The oldest Greek has no animals at all, but carved and hewn stones (see the variant).

a: one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen
p: Gold, horses from Egypt, then many wives: chapters 10–11 tick off Deuteronomy's warnings one by one.
b: Deuteronomy's law of the king says: "he must not get himself many horses, or send the people back to Egypt to get more horses" ... "He must not take many wives for himself, or his heart will turn aside. And he must not pile up great amounts of silver and gold for himself" (Deuteronomy 17:16–17). Chapter 10 piles up gold (10:14–22), silver "like the stones" (10:27) and horses from Egypt (10:28); chapter 11 adds the wives whose love turns his heart (11:1–4). Many readers think the narrator is quietly building a case against Solomon at the height of his glory. Others read chapter 10 as straightforward praise, with the turn coming only in 11:1.

a: The horses Solomon had came out of Egypt and out of Que
p: Que is Cilicia in southern Turkey. Some think 'Egypt' here hides Musri, a land near it.
b: Que (Assyrian Qu'e) was the plain of Cilicia, famous for its horses. Because Egypt was never known for horse breeding, Hugo Winckler suggested over a century ago that Mitsrayim here stands for Musri, a kingdom in the Taurus mountains named in Assyrian texts. Most scholars now keep "Egypt," noting that 10:29 speaks of chariots, which Egypt did export, and that Deuteronomy 17:16 warns against horses from Egypt. The KJV reads "linen yarn" here ("and linen yarn: the king's merchants received the linen yarn at a price"). It took miqweh as a common noun, from a root meaning "gather" or "cord," not as a place name; the Greek has a place name, Thekoue. Modern versions read "from Que" (the letters allow it), because Assyrian texts name a land Qu'e in Cilicia that was known for horses, and that fits a trade in horses and chariots far better than yarn. The picture is of Solomon's agents as middlemen in an arms trade between Egypt, Anatolia and the Syrian kingdoms.

a: the kings of the Hittites
p: Not the old Hittite empire, which had fallen, but small kingdoms in Syria that kept the Hittite name.
b: The Hittite empire of Anatolia collapsed about 1180 BC. In the following centuries a string of city-kingdoms in northern Syria and southern Turkey, such as Carchemish and Hamath, kept Hittite traditions and were called "Hatti" by the Assyrians. These are the "kings of the Hittites" here and in 2 Kings 7:6. The Hittite women of 11:1 probably came from these courts.

a: many women from foreign nations
p: Royal marriages sealed treaties. The narrator judges them by Deuteronomy, not by diplomacy.
b: Historians point out that ancient kings married foreign princesses to seal alliances; every wife on this list (Egypt, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Sidon, the Hittite states) stands for a neighbor Solomon traded or made peace with. The narrator sees it differently: "Solomon gave his love" (ahav), and that love is the problem. The word nokhriyyot "foreign women" is the same one used of the "foreign woman" in Proverbs, who leads a young man away (Proverbs 2:16; Proverbs 5:20), a book tradition assigns to Solomon. Nehemiah drew the lesson later: "Him too the foreign women led into sin" (Nehemiah 13:26).

a: Do not go in among them, and they are not to come in among you
p: The command blends Exodus 34, Deuteronomy 7 and Joshua 23.
b: No single law says exactly this. Moses warned: "Do not marry into their families" (Deuteronomy 7:3), because "their daughters will chase after their gods" (Exodus 34:16). Joshua's farewell is closest: "Suppose you marry them and go in among them, and they among you" (Joshua 23:12). Those laws named the nations of Canaan; Solomon's wives come mostly from outside the land (Moab, Ammon, Edom, Sidon). Kings applies the principle widely: any marriage that brings in other gods breaks the covenant. Deuteronomy itself forbade Ammonites and Moabites from the LORD's assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3).

a: Solomon held on, out of love
p: The verb dabaq is the word for holding on to God, and for a man holding on to his wife.
b: Deuteronomy uses dabaq for Israel's loyalty to the LORD (Deuteronomy 10:20; Deuteronomy 13:4), and Joshua sets it against holding on to the nations: "hold on to the LORD your God" (Joshua 23:8) rather than "hold on to the rest of these nations" (Joshua 23:12). Genesis uses it of a man who "sticks close to his wife" (Genesis 2:24). The irony is sharp: the king clung, but to the wrong ones. The Hebrew puts "to them" first for emphasis.
orig: בָּהֶם דָּבַק שְׁלֹמֹה לְאַהֲבָה (bahem davaq Shelomoh le'ahavah)
r: Genesis 2:24; Deuteronomy 10:20; Deuteronomy 13:4; Joshua 23:8; Joshua 23:12; Ruth 1:14

a: Seven hundred wives belonged to him, women of noble rank, and three hundred concubines
p: The numbers are huge and round. Readers take them as fact, as royal legend, or as the narrator's satire.
b: The Song of Songs, also linked with Solomon, mentions "sixty are the queens and eighty the concubines" (Song of Songs 6:8). Some take the thousand as a literal harem, like those of later Persian and Ottoman rulers. Others see a round figure for limitless excess. The rabbis saw Deuteronomy's warning fulfilled to the letter. The Talmud says the reason for the law against many wives was given so that kings would know it, and Solomon reasoned, "I will take many and not turn aside," and he turned (Sanhedrin 21b). A concubine (pilegesh) was a secondary wife with fewer rights.
r: Deuteronomy 17:17; Song of Songs 6:8–9; Ecclesiastes 2:8; Nehemiah 13:26

a: By the time Solomon was old
p: The text says he 'went after' other gods. Some rabbis argued he only failed to stop his wives.
b: Kings says Solomon "went after" Ashtoreth and Milcom (11:5) and built high places (11:7). The Talmud reports a defense: "Whoever says Solomon sinned is simply mistaken"; his wives turned his heart, but he did not worship, and Scripture counts it as if he had because he did not stop them (Shabbat 56b). Most Christian and modern readers take the text at its word. Whether Solomon repented has also been debated: some church fathers held that he did and point to Ecclesiastes as his late confession; Cyril of Jerusalem, for example, counts him among those who repented (Catecheses 2.13), while others left it in doubt. The narrator says only that old age did not bring wisdom.

a: Ashtoreth, goddess of the Sidonians
p: The goddess Astarte. Hebrew writers gave her name the vowels of boshet, 'shame.'
b: Phoenician inscriptions spell her name 'shtrt, pronounced Ashtart (Greek Astarte), the great goddess of Sidon and Tyre, linked with love, war and the evening star. The Masoretic vowels of Ashtoret seem to borrow from boshet, "shame," a scribal habit also seen in names like Ish-bosheth. Hebrew has no separate word for "goddess," so the text says "god of the Sidonians." Sidon here means the Phoenicians in general, including Tyre (16:31).

a: on the mountain facing Jerusalem
p: The Mount of Olives, east of the city. Josiah tore these shrines down three centuries later.
b: "Facing Jerusalem" means east, across the Kidron Valley: the Mount of Olives or its southern ridge. 2 Kings 23:13 calls it "the Mount of Destruction" (har hammashchit), a pun on har hammishchah, "Mount of Anointing" (oil), and reports that Josiah defiled "the high places that Solomon king of Israel had built" there for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom. That the shrines stood for some 300 years shows how long Solomon's choice lasted. Chemosh was Moab's national god, known from the Mesha Stele.

a: Molech, the vile idol of the Ammonites
p: Verse 5 says Milcom is the Ammonite god. Here the Hebrew has Molech, probably a slip or a scribal blending.
b: Milcom ("their king") was the god of Ammon (11:5, 33; 2 Kings 23:13). Molech is the name tied to child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom (Leviticus 18:21; 2 Kings 23:10). The Greek translation reads "their king" here, and many scholars think the original read Milcom. Both names come from the root mlk, "king," so a scribe could easily confuse or blend them. There is no sign in Kings that Solomon sacrificed children.

a: hand it to your servant
p: The man who will take the kingdom is one of Solomon's own officials: Jeroboam (11:26).
b: Eved can mean slave, servant or royal official, depending on context. Here it points to Jeroboam, who "served Solomon" (11:26) as head of the labor gangs (11:28). The words echo Samuel's sentence on Saul, whose kingdom was given "to a neighbor of yours who is better than you" (1 Samuel 15:28). The tearing image will be acted out with a cloak in 11:30.

a: One tribe I will give your son
t: Ten tribes and one: the arithmetic
p: Ten pieces plus one tribe makes eleven, not twelve. Interpreters explain the missing tribe in several ways.
b: Ahijah tears his cloak into twelve, gives Jeroboam ten, and says one tribe will stay with David's line (11:31–32). One answer is that Benjamin was so closely joined to Judah that the two count as one (12:21). Another is that Simeon had already been absorbed into Judah (Joshua 19:1). Another is that Levi had no land and is not counted. Some medieval Jewish commentators take Judah, the king's own tribe, as assumed, and the "one" as Benjamin. The Greek solves the sum differently: at 11:32 and 11:36 it reads "two tribes," and at 12:20 "Judah and Benjamin" (see the variants). The narrator's point is the same: God leaves David a small share for David's sake and Jerusalem's.

a: The LORD stirred up an adversary for Solomon
p: Hebrew satan here means a human enemy, not the devil.
b: In Samuel and Kings a satan is any opponent: David is called one by the Philistines (1 Samuel 29:4), and Abishai by David (2 Samuel 19:22). Solomon had said, "There is no adversary, and nothing bad is happening" (5:4), using the word satan. Now God raises up two, Hadad and Rezon (11:23). The word only later became the name of a spiritual enemy, Satan, in books such as Job and Zechariah. That the LORD himself stirs up opponents is the narrator's way of saying that Solomon's troubles were judgment, not bad luck.

a: he struck down every male in Edom
p: The campaign is mentioned in 2 Samuel 8:13–14 and in the title of Psalm 60. Joab's slaughter is told only here.
b: 2 Samuel 8:13–14 reports that David struck down Edomites in the Valley of Salt and put garrisons throughout Edom. The title of Psalm 60 credits Joab with twelve thousand Edomite dead. "Every male" is surely an exaggeration, since Edom survived, but it explains Hadad's hatred. The story of a young prince saved from a massacre, raised at a foreign court, and returning to reclaim his land, follows a pattern known from the ancient world (compare Moses, Exodus 2).

a: Queen Tahpenes
p: An Egyptian king welcomes a refugee prince who might trouble Israel. Tahpenes may be a title.
b: No pharaoh named in surviving records had a wife called Tahpenes. Some Egyptologists have suggested it renders an Egyptian title, ta-hemet-nesu, "the king's wife," taken by the Hebrew writer as a name; that is possible but uncertain. The Hebrew calls her the gevirah, the "great lady" or queen mother (compare 15:13). Hosting exiled princes was a common way for Egypt to keep a hand in Asian politics, and Jeroboam later finds the same welcome (11:40).

a: took power in Damascus
p: Rezon founds the Aramean state that will be Israel's chief rival for two centuries.
b: David had defeated Hadadezer of Zobah and the Arameans of Damascus (2 Samuel 8:3–8). Rezon, one of Hadadezer's men, turned an outlaw band into a kingdom. Aram-Damascus became the strongest state in Syria in the 9th century, and its kings (Ben-hadad, Hazael) fill much of 1 Kings 15–2 Kings 13. Hezion, the grandfather of Ben-hadad in 15:18, may be the same man as Rezon, since the names are close; many scholars think so, though the evidence is thin.

a: His mother's name was Zeruah, a widow
p: 'Zeruah' sounds like 'diseased skin.' The long Greek account calls his mother Sarira, a prostitute.
b: The name Tserua resembles tsara'at, a skin disease, and many think it is a slur rather than a real name; the mothers of kings of Judah are named, but the mothers of Israel's kings almost never are. The Greek supplement at 12:24b calls her Sarira, "a woman, a prostitute." Some read these as hostile southern tradition about the founder of the northern kingdom. Others note that a widow's son rising by his own ability is a story of merit, the opposite of Rehoboam's inherited throne.

a: the breach of the City of David
p: Jeroboam's revolt started on a building site, among the forced laborers.
b: The Millo ("the fill") was probably the great stepped stone terrace on the eastern slope of the City of David, or a fill between the old city and the temple mount; its exact location is debated. Closing the "breach" may mean filling the gap between David's city and Solomon's new temple area to the north. The verse gives the setting of Jeroboam's rise: he was a foreman on Solomon's great projects, the very place where the people's resentment of forced labor gathered (12:4).

a: the house of Joseph
p: Ephraim and Manasseh, the central hill country tribes. Jeroboam was put over his own people's labor gangs.
b: "House of Joseph" means the two tribes descended from Joseph's sons, Ephraim and Manasseh (Joshua 17:17; Judges 1:22). They held the heart of the northern hill country around Shechem and Bethel. Making an Ephraimite foreman over Ephraimite laborers was efficient, but it handed Jeroboam a ready following. Joseph was also the name used by the prophets for the northern kingdom (Amos 5:6; Ezekiel 37:16).

a: Ahijah had wrapped himself in a new cloak
p: The Hebrew says 'he had covered himself.' Most read Ahijah; some read Jeroboam.
b: The subject "he" could be either man. Most interpreters, with the Greek and most translations, take it as Ahijah, who then tears his own cloak. Some Jewish and modern readers think the prophet seized Jeroboam's cloak, which would make the symbol a gift taken from Jeroboam and returned to him in part. The cloak is "new," which may picture the new kingdom, or simply show that a perfectly good garment, like a good kingdom, was being ruined. Compare Saul tearing Samuel's robe (1 Samuel 15:27–28) and David cutting Saul's (1 Samuel 24:4–5).
orig: וְהוּא מִתְכַּסֶּה בְּשַׂלְמָה חֲדָשָׁה (vehu mitkasseh besalmah chadashah)

a: ripped it into twelve pieces
p: Prophets often acted out their message. A torn cloak pictures a torn kingdom.
b: The verb qara' "tear" is the key word of the chapter (11:11, 12, 13, 31). Samuel's ripped robe meant Saul's lost kingdom (1 Samuel 15:27–28): "Today the LORD has ripped Israel's kingship off you" (1 Samuel 15:28). Later prophets act out messages in the same way: Isaiah walks barefoot, Jeremiah breaks a jar and wears a yoke, Ezekiel lies on his side (Isaiah 20:2–4; Jeremiah 19:10–11; Jeremiah 27:2; Ezekiel 4:4–6). The sign makes God's word visible and, in the prophets' view, sets it in motion.

a: a lamp will burn for David
p: Hebrew nir is usually read as 'lamp.' One scholar argued it means 'dominion.'
b: The lamp image pictures a family line that does not go out (2 Samuel 21:17; Psalm 132:17), and the phrase returns in 15:4 and 2 Kings 8:19. In 1968 Paul Hanson argued that nir here is a different word meaning "yoke" or "dominion," so that David is promised continuing rule. Most translations keep "lamp," as the Vulgate does (lucerna). The Greek here has thesis, "a placing, an establishment," which leans toward a sense like Hanson's rather than toward "lamp." Either way, the promise is that David's house will keep Jerusalem.

a: I will build you a house that lasts, the way I built one for David
p: Jeroboam is offered the same promise David received, on the same terms.
b: The phrase "a lasting house" (bayit ne'eman) is Nathan's phrase for David's dynasty (2 Samuel 7:16; 1 Samuel 25:28). Jeroboam is not a rebel in God's eyes: he is God's chosen ruler for the north, with a real chance of a lasting dynasty if he keeps the law. That makes his failure in chapter 12 the more serious. "Not for all time" (11:39) leaves the door open to a future reunion under David's line, a hope the prophets voice (Ezekiel 37:15–24; Hosea 3:5).

a: to Shishak king of Egypt
t: Shishak: the first pharaoh named in the Bible
p: Shishak is Shoshenq I, founder of Egypt's 22nd dynasty. He gives a date to anchor the chronology of Kings.
b: Before this verse every Egyptian king in the Bible is just "Pharaoh." Shishak (Egyptian Shoshenq) was a Libyan general who founded a new dynasty about 945 BC. A new ruler with no ties to Solomon's father-in-law had good reason to shelter Solomon's enemy. His campaign into Judah and Israel (14:25) is the first event in the Bible confirmed by an outside record, his victory relief at Karnak in Thebes.

a: the Scroll of Solomon's Deeds
p: Kings names three lost sources: a scroll of Solomon's deeds and court records of Israel and of Judah.
b: The narrator points readers to the Scroll of Solomon's Deeds (literally "the matters of Solomon"), and later to "the records of the kings of Israel" (14:19) and "of Judah" (14:29). These books are lost. They were probably court annals or summaries drawn from them, since Kings cites them for wars, building and plots, not for the religious verdicts. The phrase "records of the days" (divre hayyamim) is also the Hebrew title of the book of Chronicles, but Chronicles was written centuries later and is not the book meant. 1 Maccabees copies the formula for John Hyrcanus: "The rest of John's story, his wars and the brave deeds he did... look, they are written in the book of the days of his high priesthood" (1 Maccabees 16:23–24). For Judas it turns it around: his story "was never written down, for there was a great deal of it" (1 Maccabees 9:22).

a: forty years
p: Forty years, like David's reign and many periods in Judges. Most date Solomon about 970–931 BC.
b: Forty is a round number for a full generation in the Bible (Judges 3:11; 2 Samuel 5:4). Working back from fixed points in Assyrian records, the main chronologies place Solomon's death and the split of the kingdom about 931/930 BC (Thiele, Galil; Kitchen 931), about 928 (Tadmor and Cogan) or about 927/926 (Hayes and Hooker); W. F. Albright's older system gave 922. The difference comes from how the reigns of the later kings are added up; see the topic on dating the kings.

a: All Israel had come to Shechem to make him king
p: The northern tribes did not simply accept Solomon's son. They met at their own old covenant center.
b: Shechem, between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, was where Joshua renewed the covenant (Joshua 24) and where Abimelech was made king (Judges 9:6). David had become king over the northern tribes only by a covenant made with their elders at Hebron (2 Samuel 5:1–3). The meeting at Shechem suggests that the north still saw the kingship as an agreement with conditions, not an automatic inheritance. Rehoboam has to come to them.

a: Your father made our yoke a hard one
p: The people's complaint is the cost Samuel predicted when Israel first asked for a king.
b: Samuel had warned that a king "will take your sons and put them to work for himself" and that "you will end up as his slaves" (1 Samuel 8:11, 17). Solomon's forced labor (5:13–14; 9:15) and his provincial food levies (4:7) were that warning come true. The "yoke" is the image of a working animal. The tribes do not demand independence; they offer service in return for relief, a conditional loyalty that recalls 2 Samuel 5:3.

a: If you become a servant to this people today and serve them
p: The elders' advice turns the royal order upside down: serve the people, and they will serve you.
b: The elders do not ask Rehoboam to give up power, only to win loyalty by one day's humility. Their wording plays on eved "servant": be a servant, and they will be your servants. Christian readers often hear an anticipation of Jesus' teaching: "if anyone among you wishes to become great, he will be your servant. And if anyone among you wishes to be first, he will be everyone's slave" (Mark 10:43–44). Proverbs, also linked to Solomon, says "A soft-spoken answer turns fury back" (Proverbs 15:1), the advice his son ignores.

a: the boys he had grown up with
p: The Hebrew yeladim means 'children' or 'boys.' The young advisers were men about forty.
b: The narrator calls the elders zeqenim (old men, elders) and the young advisers yeladim, a word for children. Rehoboam was forty-one when he became king (14:21), so his friends were not teenagers. The word is mocking: these are courtiers who grew up in the palace and never had to work under the yoke. 2 Chronicles 13:7 calls Rehoboam himself "young and soft of heart" at the time.

a: My smallest part is thicker than my father's hips
p: Hebrew has only 'my little one.' 'Finger' is supplied by most translations. Some hear a crude boast.
b: The word qoten means "little thing" or "smallness"; "finger" is not in the text, and the familiar "my little finger" is the translators' guess, found in the Latin Vulgate and the Syriac and in Rashi's commentary; the Greek has "my littleness." Motnayim means the hips or loins, the part of the body where a belt is worn and strength is seated. Several modern commentators think the young men are coaching Rehoboam in a crude sexual boast about his manhood compared with his father's. Whether coarse or not, the line is meant to sound like the swagger of men who have never felt a yoke.
orig: קָטָנִּי עָבָה מִמָּתְנֵי אָבִי (qotanni avah mimmotne avi)

a: I will punish you with scorpions
p: Probably a barbed or knotted whip, named for the scorpion's sting.
b: Most interpreters, ancient and modern, take "scorpions" as a cruel kind of whip, with metal barbs or sharp knots that stung like a scorpion. Medieval Jewish commentators explained it as a whip set with thorns. The verb yissar means to discipline or correct, the word used for a father correcting a son (Deuteronomy 8:5; Proverbs 3:12). Rehoboam talks to free tribesmen as if they were rebellious children or slaves.

a: The LORD had brought about this turn
p: The text gives three causes at once: God's judgment, a foolish king, and old tribal resentments.
b: God's judgment. The narrator says the split was sibbah, "a turn" from the LORD, to fulfill Ahijah's word (11:29–39), and Shemaiah says "this thing has come from me" (12:24). The cause is Solomon's idolatry (11:33). A foolish king. Yet Rehoboam is fully responsible: he rejects wise counsel and answers with threats. Jewish and Christian interpreters alike have read the passage as a case of God working through free human choices, not around them (compare Genesis 50:20). Tribal politics. Historians stress older fault lines. The north had followed Saul's house against David (2 Samuel 2–4), rebelled under Sheba with the same cry (2 Samuel 20:1), and carried the heavier share of Solomon's labor. On this reading the union under David and Solomon was a personal union of two peoples that came apart when a weak heir pushed too hard.

a: What is our share in David?
p: The northern tribes shout the same slogan Sheba son of Bichri used against David.
b: Under David, Sheba "blew the ram's horn and said, 'We have no share in David, no inheritance in the son of Jesse! Everyone to his tents, Israel!'" (2 Samuel 20:1). That revolt failed; this one succeeds. "To your tents" is an old rallying cry from the time when Israel's tribes lived in tents: go home, the alliance is over. An old Jewish scribal tradition lists this verse among the "corrections of the scribes," claiming that "to your tents" (le'ohalekha) replaced an original "to your gods" (le'lohekha); most scholars doubt the claim, but it shows how early readers heard the cry as a break with the LORD as well as with David.

a: Adoram, the man over the forced labor
p: Rehoboam sends the head of forced labor to calm a revolt against forced labor.
b: Adoram is a shortened form of Adoniram, Solomon's labor chief (4:6; 5:14). An Adoram held the same post under David (2 Samuel 20:24), which means either one man served three kings for some forty years or a son followed his father in office. Chronicles calls him Hadoram (2 Chronicles 10:18). Whether he was sent to negotiate or to enforce, his stoning ends the talks. Stoning was the community's punishment for a public enemy (Joshua 7:25).

a: and so it stands to this day
p: The phrase suggests the source was written while the northern kingdom still stood, before 722 BC.
b: After 722 BC, when Assyria destroyed Samaria (2 Kings 17:6), it made little sense to say Israel was still in revolt against David's house. Many scholars therefore think the writer of Kings copied this line from an older source written while both kingdoms existed. Others read "to this day" as the separation of the northern population, which continued. The verb pasha "rebel" is a political word, used of a vassal breaking a treaty (2 Kings 1:1; 2 Kings 3:5), as if the north were a subject state breaking away.

a: No one followed the house of David except the tribe of Judah alone
p: From here on 'Israel' usually means the northern kingdom and 'Judah' the southern.
b: The north was larger, richer and more open to trade, with the best farmland and the main roads. Judah was a hill country around Jerusalem, with Benjamin as a border zone that the two kingdoms fought over for decades (15:16–22). Readers should watch the names: "Israel" can still mean all twelve tribes, but in Kings it now mostly means the ten northern tribes. Archaeologists debate how developed Judah was as a state at this time; many think it grew strong only in the 8th century.

a: a hundred and eighty thousand picked warriors
p: An army of 180,000 is far beyond what Judah could raise. Some take 'thousand' as a military unit.
b: Estimates for the whole population of Judah in the 10th century run to a few tens of thousands. Three main explanations are offered. Some accept the numbers as given. Others, following George Mendenhall, think the word elef "thousand" once meant a unit or clan contingent, so the original sense was 180 units. Others see stylized epic numbers meant to show size and importance. The same question arises throughout Kings and Chronicles (2 Chronicles 13:3 has armies of 400,000 and 800,000).

a: Shemaiah, the man of God
p: An older title for a prophet, used often in Kings for wonder-working prophets.
b: "Man of God" is used for Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1), Samuel (1 Samuel 9:6) and especially Elijah and Elisha. It stresses that the person belongs to God and carries his power. Shemaiah reappears in Chronicles, where he warns Rehoboam before Shishak's invasion and keeps a record of Rehoboam's reign (2 Chronicles 12:5–7, 15). His word here is the first time a prophet stops a war between the brother kingdoms.

a: as the LORD had said
t: The Greek's other story of Jeroboam (12:24a–z)
p: After this verse the Greek adds a long second account of Jeroboam's rise, with different details.
b: Codex Vaticanus and most Greek manuscripts add some 25 verses here, numbered 12:24a–z. They retell Jeroboam's story: his mother Sarira is a prostitute; he builds a fortress for Solomon and has 300 chariots; he marries an Egyptian princess, Ano, sister of Shishak's queen; his son falls sick and his wife consults Ahijah (the story of 14:1–18, which the Old Greek lacks in its Hebrew place); and at Shechem it is Shemaiah, not Ahijah, who tears a new garment into twelve. Some scholars (Adrian Schenker, and in part Julio Trebolle) think this account preserves an older form of the story. Others (D. W. Gooding, Zipora Talshir) see a later Jewish retelling built from the Hebrew. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew; the chapter page summarizes the Greek.

a: fortified Penuel
p: Jacob's 'face of God' across the Jordan. Jeroboam secures the east bank too.
b: Penuel (or Peniel) on the Jabbok River is where Jacob wrestled and said he had seen God face to face (Genesis 32:30–31). Gideon tore down its tower (Judges 8:17). Jeroboam's building there may have been to hold Gilead, or as a refuge: Shishak's list at Karnak names Penuel and Mahanaim among the towns his army reached. Archaeology has not confirmed which mound is Penuel.

a: Here are your gods, Israel, that brought you up from the land of Egypt!
p: Jeroboam repeats, word for word, what was said at the golden calf of Sinai.
b: At Sinai Aaron made the calf and the people said, "These are your gods, Israel, that brought you up from the land of Egypt!" (Exodus 32:4). The Hebrew of Kings uses nearly the same words (only "here" for "these"), including the strange plural "gods" with a plural verb, which suits two calves better than one. Many critical scholars think Exodus 32 was shaped as a polemic against Jeroboam's shrines. Traditional readers see Jeroboam repeating Israel's first sin on purpose or in blindness. Either way, the narrator wants readers to hear Sinai: a king who should have been a new Moses has become a new Aaron.

a: made two calves of gold
p: Did Jeroboam set up idols, or empty pedestals for the invisible LORD, like the cherubim in Jerusalem?
b: The narrator treats the calves as idols and calls them "other gods" (14:9). Hosea mocks: "a craftsman made it, and it is no god" (Hosea 8:6, fresh rendering) and "Those who sacrifice human beings kiss calves" (Hosea 13:2, fresh rendering). Many historians, following W. F. Albright, argue that Jeroboam meant the young bulls as pedestals on which the invisible LORD stood, the way the cherubim served as his throne in Jerusalem; storm gods in Syrian art often stand on bulls. Jeroboam claimed to worship the God of the exodus, not Baal. Jewish tradition counts Jeroboam among those who "have no share in the world to come" (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2) for leading Israel astray. A bronze bull from a 12th-century hilltop shrine in Samaria's hills shows that bull images were used in the region.
r: 14:9; Exodus 32:4; Hosea 8:5–6; Hosea 10:5; Hosea 13:2; 2 Kings 10:29; 2 Kings 17:16

a: He placed one calf in Bethel, and the other he put in Dan
p: Two border shrines with old roots: Jacob's Bethel in the south, the Danites' shrine in the far north.
b: Bethel, about 12 miles north of Jerusalem, was where Jacob saw the stairway and named the place (Genesis 28:19). Dan, at the springs of the Jordan, had a shrine with a priesthood descended from Moses (Judges 18:30). Jeroboam chose places with history. At Tel Dan, Avraham Biran excavated a large stone platform, a sacred precinct and a horned altar, which he dated in its first phase to the time of Jeroboam; the dating and use of the platform are debated. Bethel's remains are poorly known. Amos later calls Bethel "a king's sanctuary" (Amos 7:13).
r: Genesis 28:10–22; Judges 18:27–31; Amos 4:4; Amos 7:13; Hosea 10:5; 2 Kings 10:29

a: men who were not from the sons of Levi
p: The Levites, says Chronicles, left the north and moved to Judah.
b: Deuteronomy gives the priesthood to the tribe of Levi (Deuteronomy 18:1–5). Chronicles says that Jeroboam and his sons "rejected" the Levites from serving the LORD as priests, so the Levites left their pasturelands and moved to Judah and Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 11:14). Ironically, the priests of Dan claimed descent from Moses, a Levite (Judges 18:30). The phrase "from the general run of the people" (literally "from the ends of the people") can mean "from all ranks" or "from the lowest."

a: a house of high places
p: The Hebrew is singular: 'a house of high places.' It probably means shrine buildings in general.
b: The Hebrew beit bamot is singular, "house of high places," while the following verse speaks of many high places (12:32) and 13:32 of "the houses of the high places" in the towns of Samaria. Most translations make it plural to match. Read as a collective, it means Jeroboam built shrine buildings at hilltop sanctuaries across his kingdom, not one temple. Some think it refers first to the main sanctuary building at Bethel. The Plain English Translation keeps the singular.
orig: בֵּית בָּמוֹת (beit bamot), 'a house of high places'

a: in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month
p: Judah kept the Feast of Booths in the seventh month. Jeroboam set his in the eighth.
b: The law fixes the Feast of Booths on "the fifteenth day of this seventh month" (Leviticus 23:34). Jeroboam's feast falls a month later. The narrator sees a date "thought up out of his own heart" (12:33). Shemaryahu Talmon argued that the north may have followed an older calendar, or a harvest season that ran later in the north, so that Jeroboam restored a local custom rather than inventing one. Others think he simply wanted a calendar of his own to break the habit of pilgrimage. The feast is the setting for chapter 13.

a: he went up on the altar to burn incense
p: Jeroboam acts as his own high priest. Kings of Judah did similar things.
b: The verb "went up" is repeated, picturing the king on the ramp of the altar. Kings in the ancient world often led sacrifice, and David and Solomon offered too (2 Samuel 6:17–18; 1 Kings 9:25). Chronicles condemns King Uzziah for burning incense (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Here the act sets up the next scene: as Jeroboam stands at the altar to burn incense, a man of God interrupts (13:1).

a: by the LORD's word
p: The phrase bidvar YHWH runs through the chapter seven times. The story is about obeying God's word.
b: The chapter repeats "by the LORD's word" at 13:1, 2, 5, 9, 17, 18 and 32, and "the LORD's word" twice more (13:20, 26). The man of God comes by that word, speaks by it, is forbidden to eat by it, and is fooled by a false claim to it (13:18). Another key word is shuv, "turn back, return," which occurs sixteen times: the hand that cannot be brought back, the road he must not go back on, the prophet who brings him back, and Jeroboam who "did not turn back" (13:33). The structure makes the story a test case of who truly speaks for God.

a: His name will be Josiah
p: The prophecy names a king born about 300 years later. Readers explain this very differently.
b: Josiah reigned about 640–609 BC and did exactly this at Bethel (2 Kings 23:15–20). Traditional Jewish and Christian readers see true predictive prophecy, like the naming of Cyrus (Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1). Most critical scholars think the story, or at least the name, was written or sharpened in Josiah's time, when the first edition of Kings was likely composed to celebrate his reforms; they read it as prophecy after the event. Some mediate: an old prophetic story about an altar at Bethel was later linked to Josiah by name. The chapter's own theme, that God's word is sure to happen (13:32), is what the narrator wants readers to take away.

a: They will burn people's bones on you
p: Human bones made a holy place unclean forever. It was the worst desecration an altar could suffer.
b: Contact with the dead made a person or place unclean (Numbers 19:11–16). Burning bones on an altar turned the place of sacrifice into a place of death. Josiah did this at Bethel, taking bones from the tombs nearby (2 Kings 23:16), and the prophecy is carried out in exact detail. "Sacrifice the priests" is grim irony: the priests who sacrificed on it become the sacrifice (2 Kings 23:20).

a: the hand he had reached out against him went stiff and dry
p: Jeroboam's rise began when he 'lifted his hand against the king' (11:26). Now his hand is held fast.
b: The verb yavesh "dry up" is used of withered plants. The hand that gives orders cannot even come back to the king's own body. It is the same word play as 11:26–27, where Jeroboam "lifted his hand" against Solomon. The sign shows who rules at Bethel: not the king who built the altar, but the LORD who sent the prophet. A king who reaches for a prophet and is struck recurs in 2 Kings 1:9–12 and 2 Chronicles 16:10.

a: Please beg the LORD your God to soften
p: Hebrew: 'soften the face of the LORD.' It is the phrase used of Moses pleading after the golden calf.
b: The idiom chillah et pene, literally "make the face soft," means to plead for favor. It is used when "Moses begged the LORD his God to soften" (Exodus 32:11) after Aaron's calf. Here Jeroboam, who has just set up calves, has to ask for the same intercession. Note that the king calls the LORD "your God," as Saul did to Samuel (1 Samuel 15:30). The healing shows mercy even to the man who made the shrine; it is an invitation to turn back that he refuses (13:33).

a: I will not eat any bread or drink any water in this place
p: Eating together meant friendship. The man of God must show that Bethel is under a curse.
b: Sharing a meal created a bond in the ancient world; to eat at a king's table meant accepting his favor (2 Samuel 9:7; 2 Kings 25:29). The command not to eat or drink in Bethel turns the prophet into a living sign: this place is unclean, like a town under the ban (Deuteronomy 13:16–17). Not going back the same way may also be a sign: the word does not return empty (Isaiah 55:11), or simply that he must leave no path for anyone to follow. Rabbinic and medieval commentators note that the man of God passes the king's test but fails the prophet's.

a: An old prophet lived in Bethel
p: A prophet living by Jeroboam's shrine, who lies and then speaks a true word. Readers judge him differently.
b: Josephus calls him a false prophet who later talked Jeroboam out of fearing the sign, saying the altar broke because it was new and the king's hand failed from tiredness (Antiquities 8.243–245); Josephus also names the man of God Jadon. The Talmud discusses him under the law of the false prophet (Sanhedrin 89a–b) and notes that the bread he offered was the occasion of a true word coming to him (Sanhedrin 103b). Many modern readers see him as a real prophet who lied to test, or to bring, a rival to his home, perhaps out of jealousy, and who is changed by what happens. The text gives no motive, which is part of its power.

a: sitting under the oak
p: The man of God has stopped to rest, not far out of town. 'The oak' is a known landmark.
b: The Hebrew ha'elah is a large terebinth or oak, the kind of tree that marked holy places and graves (Genesis 35:8; Judges 6:11). The definite article suggests a known tree on the road. The man of God has not hurried home; he is sitting, and that pause gives the old prophet his chance. Some commentators note that the command was not to eat "in this place" (13:8), and he may have been unsure whether a meal outside Bethel's walls counted.

a: An angel spoke to me by the LORD's word
t: A lie in an angel's name
p: The lie claims a newer revelation, from an angel, to cancel the word God gave directly.
b: The man of God had heard the LORD's word himself; the old prophet claims only that an angel (mal'akh, messenger) told him. The story teaches what Deuteronomy says: a sign or a claim to revelation is not enough if it leads away from what God has commanded (Deuteronomy 13:1–3), for "the LORD your God is testing you" (Deuteronomy 13:3). Paul writes in the same spirit: "if we ourselves, or even an angel from heaven, should tell you good news that is at odds with what we told you, let him be accursed" (Galatians 1:8).

a: the LORD's word came to the prophet who had brought him back
t: A true word from a liar
p: God speaks through the man who lied. Prophecy in Kings does not depend on the prophet's goodness.
b: The man who lied about an angel now receives a real word. The point is not that lying is rewarded but that God's word is not owned by any prophet: it can come through Balaam (Numbers 22–24), through a lying prophet, or through Caiaphas (John 11:49–51). Karl Barth read the chapter as a parable of the two kingdoms: the man of God from Judah and the prophet of Israel, elect and rejected, each needing the other, and finally buried in one grave (13:31). That reading is theological rather than historical, but it takes the strange story seriously as a whole.

a: Your corpse will not come to your ancestors' grave
p: To be buried far from the family tomb was a lasting disgrace.
b: Israelites hoped to be "gathered to their people" in the family tomb (Genesis 49:29–31; 2 Samuel 19:37). The man of God will lie in a stranger's grave in Bethel. Yet the old prophet gives him his own tomb and asks to be buried with him (13:30–31), and three centuries later that shared grave protects both men's bones when Josiah burns the others (2 Kings 23:17–18).

a: The donkey stood beside it, and the lion stood beside the corpse too
t: The lion that did not eat
p: A lion that kills but does not eat, and does not touch the donkey, is plainly sent.
b: Lions lived in the thickets of Israel until the Middle Ages and are a common danger in the Bible (Judges 14:5; 1 Samuel 17:34; Amos 3:12). A lion that kills a man and then stands guard over the body, leaving the donkey alone, is no accident: it is God's agent. The scene is quiet and strange, and the narrator repeats it three times (13:24, 25, 28). Lions punish disobedience again in 20:35–36 and in 2 Kings 17:25–26.

a: That is the man of God who rebelled against what the LORD said
p: The man of God was deceived, yet he dies, while the liar lives. Readers have long found this hard.
b: Many interpreters answer that he had a direct command and should not have set it aside for a secondhand report; a prophet, of all people, had to obey the word himself. Some point out that his death made the prophecy against Bethel more credible: if God would not spare his own messenger, he would surely not spare the altar. Others, especially modern readers, admit the story is meant to be disturbing, a warning about how serious God's word is. The old prophet's grief (13:30) shows the narrator does not treat it lightly. The liar's punishment is to carry the dead man home and to live with what he has done.

a: Oh, my brother!
p: Hoy achi, 'Alas, my brother!', was the standard cry of mourning.
b: Jeremiah quotes the same lament, saying that no one will mourn King Jehoiakim with "Alas, my brother" (Jeremiah 22:18). The cry hoy later became the prophets' "Woe!" Calling the man of God "my brother" may also be the old prophet's confession that they were brothers in calling, even across the border of two kingdoms.

a: in the towns of Samaria
p: Samaria was not built until Omri's time (16:24). The phrase looks back from a later day.
b: Omri founded the city of Samaria about fifty years after Jeroboam (16:24), and only later did "Samaria" become the name of the whole northern region, as in 2 Kings 17:24 and 23:19. Here the old prophet speaks in the language of the narrator's own day. Traditional readers allow that the narrator updated the name for his readers; critical readers see a sign that the story took its final form late. Either way, it ties the prophecy to the region that Assyria later called Samerina.

a: he installed as one of the priests
p: The Hebrew idiom for ordaining a priest is 'to fill his hand.'
b: "Filling the hand" is the standard phrase for installing a priest (Exodus 28:41; Exodus 29:9; Judges 17:5, 12). It may come from putting the first portions of the offering into the new priest's hands. Jeroboam ordained anyone who wanted the job, perhaps for a fee (2 Chronicles 13:9 says for a bull and seven rams).
orig: יְמַלֵּא אֶת־יָדוֹ (yemalle et-yado), 'he filled his hand'

a: This matter became the sin of Jeroboam's house
p: From here to the fall of Samaria, every northern king is judged by Jeroboam's sin.
b: The phrase "the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, which he made Israel sin" becomes the refrain for every king of the north (15:26, 34; 16:19, 26, 31; 22:52). The narrator's final account of the north's destruction ends with it: "Jeroboam pushed Israel away from following the LORD and led them into a great sin" (2 Kings 17:21). In this view the northern kingdom's ruin began at its founding, with worship set up apart from Jerusalem.

a: Jeroboam's son Abijah fell ill
p: The oldest Greek text lacks 14:1–20 here. It tells a different version inside its long addition at 12:24.
b: Codex Vaticanus has no 14:1–20 at this point (see the variant at 14:1). The story of the sick son appears instead in 12:24g–n, before Jeroboam becomes king: his wife is the Egyptian princess Ano, she goes to Ahijah without a disguise, and the prophecy is shorter. Scholars who think the Greek supplement is old see here an earlier, simpler version of the tale; those who think it is a later retelling see it borrowing from this chapter. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew order.

a: change your looks
p: A disguise fails again and again in these books. You cannot hide from a prophet.
b: Saul disguised himself to visit the medium at Endor: he "made himself unrecognizable by putting on different clothes" (1 Samuel 28:8). In 20:38 a prophet disguises himself to trap Ahab, and Ahab disguises himself in battle and still dies (22:30–34). Here the queen disguises herself to visit a prophet who is blind, and God tells him who she is before she knocks. Jeroboam's fear of being known shows he knows how far he has strayed from the prophet who made him king.

a: Go to Shiloh.
p: Shiloh held the tent and the ark in the days of Eli. Later prophets remembered its fall as a warning.
b: The tent of meeting stood at Shiloh in Joshua's time (Joshua 18:1), and Eli served there with the ark (1 Samuel 1–4). Ahijah keeps the old sanctuary's prophetic line alive in the north. Later Shiloh's ruin became a byword: the psalmist says God abandoned his dwelling at Shiloh (Psalm 78:60), and Jeremiah warns that the temple in Jerusalem will go the way of Shiloh (Jeremiah 7:12–14; 26:6). Jeroboam sends his wife back to the place where an earlier house of priests lost God's favor.
r: Joshua 18:1; 1 Samuel 1:3; 1 Samuel 4:1–11; Psalm 78:60; Jeremiah 7:12–14; Jeremiah 26:6

a: Take along ten loaves, some biscuits and a jar of honey
p: People brought food to a prophet they consulted. A plain gift fits the disguise of a common woman.
b: Saul's servant worried that they had "no present we can bring the man of God" (1 Samuel 9:7). Ben-hadad sends Elisha forty camel-loads (2 Kings 8:9). Bread, a few nikkudim (dry, crumbly cakes or biscuits) and honey are a farmer's gift, not a queen's. The Greek supplement at 12:24h has her take loaves, cakes for the prophet's children and a bunch of grapes.

a: his eyes had gone fixed with old age
p: A blind old prophet sees more than the sighted king. The Bible's pattern of blind elders.
b: Like Isaac (Genesis 27:1) and Eli (1 Samuel 3:2; 1 Samuel 4:15), Ahijah is old and cannot see. Eli's dim eyes matched a time when "The LORD's word was rare in those days; no vision was breaking out" (1 Samuel 3:1); Ahijah's blindness, by contrast, only highlights how clearly God shows him what is hidden. The verb qamu "stood still, became fixed" describes eyes that no longer move or focus.

a: me you threw behind your back
p: A strong image of contempt: to throw something behind you is to forget it on purpose.
b: The Hebrew puts "me" first for emphasis. The same image appears in Nehemiah's prayer ("they threw your law behind their back," Nehemiah 9:26) and in Ezekiel 23:35. In Isaiah 38:17 it is used the other way: God throws Hezekiah's sins behind his back. "Images of cast metal" (massekhot) is the word used for Aaron's calf (Exodus 32:4, "a calf of cast metal"), so the reference is to the calves of Bethel and Dan.
orig: וְאֹתִי הִשְׁלַכְתָּ אַחֲרֵי גַוֶּךָ (ve'oti hishlakhta achare gavvekha)

a: I will cut off every male of Jeroboam's in Israel
p: The Hebrew says 'one who urinates against a wall,' a crude phrase for every male.
b: The phrase occurs six times, mostly in curses on a royal house (14:10; 16:11; 21:21; 2 Kings 9:8); it first appears in David's oath against the household of Nabal (1 Samuel 25:22, 34). The KJV kept it ("him that pisseth against the wall"). It is vulgar on purpose: the prophet speaks of the king's sons the way soldiers speak of the enemy. The Plain English Translation gives the meaning, "every male," and leaves the image in this note.

a: the one shut in and the one set free
p: An old pair of words of uncertain sense: slave and free, minor and adult, or protected and abandoned.
b: The pair occurs again in 21:21, Deuteronomy 32:36 and 2 Kings 9:8; 14:26. Suggested meanings include "slave and free," "under age and of age," "under a ban and free," or "held back (at home) and let go (to war)." Whatever the exact sense, the pair is a way of saying "everyone, without exception." The Plain English Translation keeps the literal pair because no one sense is certain.

a: the dogs will eat
p: An unburied body was the worst fate in the ancient world. The curse returns for Baasha and Ahab.
b: Dogs in ancient towns were half-wild scavengers, not pets. To be eaten by dogs or vultures meant being denied burial, and with it a place among one's ancestors. The same sentence is passed on the houses of Baasha (16:4) and Ahab (21:24), and on Jezebel (2 Kings 9:10, 36). Ancient treaty curses threaten the same thing (Deuteronomy 28:26).

a: something good toward the LORD, the God of Israel, was found
p: The text does not say. The rabbis suggested he defied his father to let pilgrims reach Jerusalem.
b: The narrator leaves the good thing unnamed. The Talmud gives two views (Moed Katan 28b): one, that Abijah left his post on the border, where his father had placed guards to stop Israelites going up to Jerusalem, and went up on pilgrimage himself; the other, that he removed his father's guards from the road so that others could go. Others suggest simply that the child was too young to have done evil. The irony is painful: the only one of Jeroboam's house who pleased God is the one who dies first, and his death is the mercy of a proper burial and real mourning.

a: And what am I saying? It is already now
p: The Hebrew is very compressed: 'this the day, and what? even now.' Its exact sense is uncertain.
b: Translators guess. Some take it as "This is the day; what more? Even now" (the judgment begins already with the boy's death). Others read "Today, and what then? Even now," or think a few words were lost. The king God "will set up" is Baasha, who wiped out Jeroboam's house within a few years of Jeroboam's death (15:27–29).
orig: זֶה הַיּוֹם וּמֶה גַּם־עָתָּה (zeh hayyom umeh gam-attah)

a: scatter them beyond the River
t: The exile of the north foretold
p: The 'River' is the Euphrates. The northern tribes were deported to Assyria two centuries later.
b: Assyria took Samaria in 722 BC and settled the Israelites "in Halah, by the Habor River of Gozan, and in the towns of Media" (2 Kings 17:6), all beyond the Euphrates. The image of a reed shaking in water pictures a people with no root. Prophecies like this one are a main reason critical scholars think Kings in its final form was written after the exile; traditional readers see the prophecy fulfilled. Asherah poles were wooden posts or stylized trees sacred to the goddess Asherah (Deuteronomy 16:21, "an Asherah pole").

a: she came to Tirzah
p: Jeroboam's capital moved from Shechem to Tirzah, a city northeast of Shechem.
b: Tirzah was famous for its beauty (Song of Songs 6:4) and served as the northern capital until Omri built Samaria (16:23–24). It is usually identified with Tell el-Far'ah North, about 7 miles northeast of Shechem, excavated by Roland de Vaux from 1946 to 1960. He found a 10th–9th-century town, an unfinished building that some have linked with Omri's move to Samaria.

a: His mother was Naamah the Ammonite
p: Every later king of Judah descended from an Ammonite woman, as David descended from a Moabite.
b: Kings names the mother of each king of Judah, perhaps because of the queen mother's role at court (15:13). Naamah was presumably one of Solomon's foreign wives (11:1). Deuteronomy barred Ammonites and Moabites from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3), yet the royal line runs through Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite. The Talmud draws the link: God spared Ammon and Moab for the sake of "two good doves" who would come from them, Ruth and Naamah (Bava Kamma 38b), and the law was read as barring Ammonite men but not women (Yevamot 76b–77a).

a: Rehoboam was forty-one years old at the start of his reign
p: Forty-one means he was born before Solomon became king. The Greek supplement says he was sixteen.
b: If Rehoboam was forty-one when Solomon died after a forty-year reign, he was born a year before Solomon took the throne, which would make Naamah one of Solomon's first wives, married while David was alive. The Greek supplement at 12:24a says he was sixteen and reigned twelve years, which fits the picture of "the boys" around him (12:8). Most scholars follow the Hebrew; a few think the Greek preserves an older figure.

a: on every high hill and under every leafy tree
p: A stock phrase of Deuteronomy and the prophets for worship at open-air shrines.
b: Deuteronomy orders Israel to destroy the places where the nations worshiped "on the high mountains, on the hills, and under every leafy tree" (Deuteronomy 12:2). Hosea, Jeremiah and Ezekiel use the phrase for Israel's own shrines (Hosea 4:13; Jeremiah 2:20; Ezekiel 6:13). Standing stones (matsevot) were upright stones marking a holy place; the patriarchs set them up (Genesis 28:18), but Deuteronomy forbids them beside the LORD's altar (Deuteronomy 16:22). Archaeologists have found such stones at Arad and other shrines.
r: Deuteronomy 12:2–3; Deuteronomy 16:21–22; Genesis 28:18; Hosea 4:13; Jeremiah 2:20; 2 Kings 17:10

a: There were also shrine men in the land
p: The Hebrew qadesh means 'consecrated one.' The old rendering 'male cult prostitutes' is now widely questioned.
b: The word comes from the root "holy" and means a person set apart for a shrine; Deuteronomy uses it in the law "no son of Israel a shrine man" (Deuteronomy 23:17). The KJV rendered it "sodomites" and many modern versions "male shrine prostitutes," assuming that Canaanite religion practiced ritual sex. Stephanie Budin and others have argued that there is little ancient evidence for sacred prostitution at all; on that view the qedeshim were cult servants of some kind whose duties are unknown. Deuteronomy 23:18 links the word with a prostitute's fee, so some sexual sense remains possible. The Plain English Translation keeps a neutral "shrine men."

a: Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem
t: Shishak's raid and the Karnak relief
p: Pharaoh Shoshenq I recorded his campaign on a temple wall at Karnak. Jerusalem is not clearly on the list.
b: On the Bubastite Portal of the temple of Amun at Karnak, Shoshenq I is shown smiting captives above rows of name-rings listing some 150 places. Readable names include Gibeon, Beth-horon, Aijalon, Megiddo, Taanach, Mahanaim and Penuel, and many places in the Negev. A fragment of a Shoshenq stele was found at Megiddo. Jerusalem's name is not preserved; parts of the list are damaged. Many scholars think Rehoboam paid tribute (14:26) so the city was spared and not listed. Others note that the raid hit Jeroboam's Israel at least as hard as Judah, though Kings mentions only Judah. The date, about 925 BC, is one of the anchors of biblical chronology. The written Hebrew spells the name Shushaq; the reading tradition, Shishaq.

a: He even took all the gold shields Solomon had made
p: Within five years of Solomon's death, his gold is gone. The bronze copies are kept locked up.
b: Solomon's gold shields (10:16–17) were the symbol of his glory. Their replacement with bronze ones, carried out only for the king's walk to the temple and then locked in the guardroom (14:28), makes a quiet picture of decline. Chronicles adds a lesson: Shishak came "because they had been unfaithful to the LORD," and when Rehoboam and the leaders humbled themselves, God spared them from destruction but made them Shishak's servants (2 Chronicles 12:2, 6–8, fresh rendering). Temples and palaces were the treasuries of ancient states, and they are emptied again and again in Kings (15:18; 2 Kings 12:18; 2 Kings 18:15–16).

a: His son Abijam became king in his place
p: Kings calls him Abijam; Chronicles and Matthew call him Abijah. Several explanations are offered.
b: Abijah means "my father is the LORD (Yah)." Abijam may mean "father of the sea" or "my father is Yam," and some think the narrator changed a good name to a doubtful one for a bad king. Others think it is a simple scribal variant: the Greek reads Abiou here, and Chronicles uses Abijah throughout (2 Chronicles 13:1). Matthew's genealogy has Abijah (Matthew 1:7).

a: in the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam son of Nebat
t: Dating the kings by each other
p: From here on Kings dates each king by the other kingdom's reign. The numbers do not always add up.
b: Each new reign is dated by the year of the king next door (a "synchronism") and given a length. Added up, the figures for Israel and Judah drift apart by decades, and some synchronisms contradict the lengths. Edwin Thiele (1951; 3rd ed. 1983) explained most of the differences by co-regencies (father and son ruling together), by two ways of counting a king's first partial year, and by calendars that began in different months; his dates (split of the kingdom 931/930 BC) are widely used, especially by conservative scholars. Gershon Galil reaches the same date for the split by a revised system, and K. A. Kitchen also gives 931. Hayim Tadmor, followed by Mordechai Cogan, puts it about 928. John Hayes and Paul Hooker reject co-regencies and allow for scribal errors, which gives about 927/926. W. F. Albright's older and independent system (1945) put it in 922. Many critics think the numbers came from different sources and some are simply errors. No system fits every figure.

a: His mother's name was Maacah, Abishalom's daughter
p: Abishalom is probably Absalom, David's son. Chronicles calls Abijah's mother Micaiah daughter of Uriel.
b: Chronicles says Rehoboam married "Maacah daughter of Absalom" (2 Chronicles 11:20–21), so Abishalom is a longer spelling of Absalom. Since Absalom's only named child was a daughter Tamar (2 Samuel 14:27), many think "daughter" means granddaughter, through Tamar. Elsewhere Chronicles says of Abijah, "His mother's name was Micaiah, Uriel's daughter, from Gibeah" (2 Chronicles 13:2), perhaps a different form of the name and the actual father. The same Maacah is called Asa's mother in 15:10; see the note there.

a: the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem
p: God keeps David's line burning even through a bad king. See 11:36.
b: The promise of 11:36 is applied: Abijam is not like David, but for David's sake his son follows him. Kings uses this formula at the darkest moments of Judah's history (2 Kings 8:19). The verse explains the difference between the two kingdoms in this book: Israel's dynasties fall one after another, while Judah keeps a single line for over three centuries.

a: There was war between Abijam and Jeroboam
t: A bad king or a defender of the temple?
