p: Kings gives Abijam eight lines and a bad verdict. Chronicles gives him a great speech and a victory.
b: In 2 Chronicles 13, Abijah stands on Mount Zemaraim and preaches to Jeroboam's army about the LORD's covenant with David and the true priests in Jerusalem; then Judah wins a great battle and takes Bethel. Kings says only that he walked in his father's sins. Some harmonize: a king can have a sound public stance and a poor private faith. Many critical scholars see the Chronicler using Abijah to voice his own view of the temple. The two portraits show how each book chooses and shapes its material.

a: His mother's name was Maacah, Abishalom's daughter
p: Maacah is called the mother of both Abijam and Asa. 'Mother' here probably means grandmother, or queen mother.
b: Hebrew em "mother" can be used of a grandmother, as av "father" is of any ancestor (15:11, "his forefather David"). Some translations print "grandmother" here, but the Hebrew says "mother," and the Plain English Translation keeps it. One view: Maacah was Asa's grandmother and kept the queen mother's rank because Abijam reigned only three years. Another: Asa was Abijam's brother, not his son. Another: two different Maacahs. The Greek supports this last view: it calls Asa's mother Ana (15:10, 15:13) but Abijam's mother Maacah (15:2). The queen mother's office explains why Asa had to remove her (15:13).
orig: וְשֵׁם אִמּוֹ (veshem immo), 'and his mother's name'

a: all the filthy idols
p: Gillulim is a scornful word for idols, perhaps formed from gel, 'dung.'
b: The word occurs about fifty times, mostly in Ezekiel, always with contempt. It is probably related to gel "dung" or galal "round thing, pellet," and was perhaps pointed to sound like shiqqutsim, "vile things" (11:5). A plain rendering would be "dung-gods." Asa's reform is the first of the reforms by good kings of Judah that the narrator praises (2 Kings 18:4; 2 Kings 23:4–14).

a: He even took away the rank of queen mother from Maacah his mother
p: The gevirah, the king's mother, held real power at court. Asa demoted his own.
b: Gevirah means "great lady." Bathsheba sat on a throne at Solomon's right hand (2:19), and the mothers of Judah's kings are named in each reign. Jeremiah addresses "the king and the queen mother" together (Jeremiah 13:18). Hittite and Ugaritic queen mothers also held official rank and could be removed. Asa's act was a public break with the religion of his own family.

a: a horrid thing for Asherah
p: Mifletset, 'a thing to shudder at,' is a rare word. Jerome's Latin Bible guessed an obscene image.
b: The root palats means to shudder. The word appears only here and in the parallel, 2 Chronicles 15:16. What the object was is unknown: perhaps a carved image or pole for the goddess Asherah. Jerome's Vulgate (about AD 400) translated "the chief of the rites of Priapus," a Roman fertility god, and his "idol" as "simulacrum turpissimum," "most shameful image," reflecting a guess that it was phallic. The Kidron Valley, east of Jerusalem, was where later reformers burned and dumped cult objects (2 Kings 23:4, 6, 12).

a: The high places were not taken away
t: Did Asa remove the high places?
p: Kings says no. One verse in Chronicles says yes, another says no.
b: "The high places were not taken away" becomes a refrain for otherwise good kings of Judah (22:43; 2 Kings 12:3; 2 Kings 14:4; 2 Kings 15:4, 35) until Hezekiah and Josiah. 2 Chronicles 14:3–5 says Asa removed "the high places," while 2 Chronicles 15:17 agrees with Kings that they were not removed "from Israel." A common harmonization: Asa removed the high places of foreign gods but not the local shrines to the LORD; or Chronicles' "Israel" means the northern towns Asa held. The underlying standard is Deuteronomy's one chosen place of worship (Deuteronomy 12:5, 13–14).
r: 22:43; 2 Kings 12:3; 2 Kings 18:4; Deuteronomy 12:5; Deuteronomy 12:13–14; 2 Chronicles 14:3–5; 2 Chronicles 15:17

a: built up Ramah
p: Ramah lies only about five miles north of Jerusalem. Holding it choked the road to the capital.
b: Ramah (modern er-Ram) sat on the main north–south ridge road. Fortifying it cut Jerusalem's trade and travel northward and threatened the city itself. The two kingdoms fought over the tribe of Benjamin, the land between them, for decades; the line that Asa finally fixed at Geba and Mizpah (15:22) roughly marked the border for the next two centuries.

a: Ben-hadad son of Tabrimmon, son of Hezion, the king of Aram
p: 'Son of Hadad' was a throne name used by several kings of Damascus. Outside evidence for this one is disputed.
b: Hadad was the storm god of Aram (the same god called Baal by the Canaanites), so Ben-hadad means "son of Hadad." At least two and probably three Damascus kings bore the name (15:18; 20:1; 2 Kings 13:3). A stone stele found near Aleppo, dedicated to the god Melqart by a king named Bar-Hadad (about 800 BC), was once read by W. F. Albright as naming "Bar-Hadad son of Tabrimmon son of Hezion," this very king. Most scholars now reject that reading of the damaged lines, so the stele is not secure evidence for this verse.

a: a payment of silver and gold
p: The Hebrew word shochad is the usual word for a bribe.
b: In the law shochad is the bribe that "blinds the eyes" of judges (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19). In diplomacy it means a payment to buy a king's action, as when Ahaz pays Assyria (2 Kings 16:8). Calling it a "present" softens what Asa did: he paid a foreign king with the temple's treasure to break his treaty with Israel. Chronicles reports that the seer Hanani rebuked him: "Because you leaned on the king of Aram and did not lean on the LORD your God, that is why the king of Aram's army got away from you" (2 Chronicles 16:7).

a: Let a covenant stand between me and you
t: A treaty that is, or a treaty proposed?
p: The Hebrew has no verb. It can state a treaty that exists or propose one: 'let there be.'
b: The clause is literally "a covenant between me and you, between my father and your father." Many translations read it as a statement ("there is a treaty"), Asa reminding Ben-hadad of an existing alliance. Others read it as a wish or proposal ("let there be a treaty"), Asa offering a new one modeled on their fathers' ties. The rest of the verse fits both: Ben-hadad must break his treaty with Baasha in either case. The Plain English Translation takes the proposal reading ("let a covenant stand"), which suits a payment sent to win the king over.
orig: בְּרִית בֵּינִי וּבֵינֶךָ (berit beini uveineka), 'a covenant between me and you'

a: to fortify Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah
p: At Tell en-Nasbeh, probably Mizpah, a huge wall survives from about this time.
b: Mizpah is usually identified with Tell en-Nasbeh, about 8 miles north of Jerusalem, where excavators found a massive city wall, up to 4 meters thick, with a strong gate; many date it to the 9th century and connect it with Asa. Jeremiah mentions the great cistern "King Asa had made because of Baasha king of Israel" (Jeremiah 41:9, fresh rendering). The Talmud read "with no one excused" as Asa's fault: he drafted even students of the law for his building, and his foot disease was the punishment (Sotah 10a).

a: he got a sickness in his feet
p: Chronicles says he sought doctors, not the LORD. Commentators guess gout, gangrene or a euphemism.
b: 2 Chronicles 16:12 adds that the disease was severe and that "even in his illness he did not seek the LORD, but the physicians" (fresh rendering). Medical guesses include gout, circulation failure with gangrene, or swelling from heart disease. A few think "feet" is a polite word for the genitals, as sometimes in Hebrew (Isaiah 7:20), but nothing here requires it. The rabbis linked it to his forced labor policy (Sotah 10a, see 15:22). The Chronicler's remark is not a ban on doctors, but on trusting them in place of God.

a: Baasha son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, plotted against him
p: Jeroboam's dynasty ends with his son, at a siege. Israel's kings will fall to coups again and again.
b: Nadab reigned two years. Baasha came from Issachar, in the Jezreel Valley, while Jeroboam was from Ephraim; tribal rivalry may lie behind the coup. Gibbethon, a town on the border of the Philistine plain (Joshua 19:44), was still being besieged twenty-five years later (16:15), which suggests a long and costly frontier war. In its two centuries the northern kingdom had nine dynasties, against Judah's one, and most changes came by assassination.

a: as the LORD's word had said through his servant Ahijah the Shilonite
p: Kings is built on a chain of prophecies and their fulfillments.
b: Ahijah's word (14:10–11) comes true under Baasha; Jehu's word against Baasha (16:1–4) comes true under Zimri (16:12); the man of God's word comes true under Josiah (2 Kings 23:16). Gerhard von Rad called this pattern the backbone of the Deuteronomistic History: history is the working out of God's spoken word. Critical scholars note that this does not excuse Baasha, who killed for his own ambition (16:7); traditional readers see God's sovereignty and human guilt held together, as at the split (12:15).

a: Baasha son of Ahijah took the throne over all Israel at Tirzah, for twenty-four years
p: Chronicles says Baasha attacked Judah in Asa's 36th year. By Kings' count Baasha was dead ten years before that.
b: Baasha began in Asa's third year and reigned twenty-four years, so he died about Asa's twenty-sixth year (16:8). Yet 2 Chronicles 16:1 dates the building of Ramah to Asa's thirty-sixth year. Thiele and others suggest the Chronicler counted from the division of the kingdom (the thirty-sixth year of Judah as a kingdom), which would fit Asa's sixteenth. Others think the numbers in Chronicles were miscopied, or reflect the Chronicler's scheme of blessing and decline in Asa's life. The puzzle is a standard example in the debate over the dates of the kings.

a: Jehu son of Hanani
p: Not King Jehu of 2 Kings 9. This Jehu was a prophet whose father Hanani rebuked King Asa.
b: Jehu son of Hanani is the only prophet of Baasha's time named in Kings. Chronicles says he later rebuked Jehoshaphat of Judah (2 Chronicles 19:2) and wrote a history of Jehoshaphat's reign (2 Chronicles 20:34). His father Hanani the seer rebuked Asa (2 Chronicles 16:7). If the dates are right, Jehu's career spanned some fifty years and both kingdoms. He is a different man from Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, the army officer who became king (2 Kings 9:2).

a: I raised you up out of the dust
p: The phrase is Hannah's: God lifts the poor from the dust and seats them with princes.
b: Hannah sang that the LORD "lifts the poor up out of the dust" (1 Samuel 2:8) and gives them a seat among nobles. Baasha was a man of no royal family whom God made ruler (nagid, the title used for Saul and David). Like Jeroboam (14:7), he was given the throne as a gift and misused it. Psalm 113:7–8 repeats Hannah's words.

a: and also because he struck that house down
t: Punished for doing what was foretold?
p: Baasha fulfilled Ahijah's prophecy by destroying Jeroboam's house, yet he is condemned for it.
b: The last clause is surprising: God foretold the end of Jeroboam's house (14:10), yet Baasha is judged for carrying it out. Most interpreters, Jewish and Christian, answer that Baasha did not act in obedience to God but out of his own ambition, and then kept Jeroboam's sins; God can use a violent man's deeds without approving them (compare Isaiah 10:5–15, where Assyria is God's rod and still punished). The same tension appears with King Jehu: he wipes out Ahab's house at a prophet's command (2 Kings 9–10), yet Hosea announces, in God's words, "In a very little while I will bring the blood shed at Jezreel down on the house of Jehu" (Hosea 1:4, fresh rendering). Some critics read the verse as a later editor's addition to 16:1–4.

a: drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza
t: A king drunk while the army fights
p: Elah drinks at his steward's house while the army besieges Gibbethon. His chariot commander strikes.
b: Elah's reign lasted barely a year (Asa's 26th to 27th year). The army was in the field at Gibbethon (16:15), and the king was at a party. Arza was "over the house," the palace steward, an office known from Solomon's court (4:6) and from a seal impression and a tomb inscription of later stewards. Zimri commanded half the chariots, a powerful post in a kingdom whose army relied on chariotry (22:31). The scene recalls Ben-hadad drinking while his army is routed (20:16) and Belshazzar's feast (Daniel 5).

a: not a relative who could avenge him
p: The Hebrew go'el is the kinsman who protects or avenges a family member.
b: A go'el was the close relative who redeemed land, freed a kinsman from slavery, married a widow to keep a family name (as Boaz did for Ruth), or avenged a murdered relative (Numbers 35:19). Zimri kills even these, so no one is left with the duty to avenge Baasha's family. The same word is used of God himself as Israel's Redeemer (Isaiah 41:14). On "a single male," see 14:10.

a: with their puffs of air
p: Hebrew hevel means vapor or breath. Idols are as empty as a breath.
b: Hevel is the word Ecclesiastes uses over and over: "Vapor of vapors! Everything is vapor" (Ecclesiastes 1:2; the site renders hevel "vapor"), often translated "vanity" or "meaningless." Applied to idols it means things with no substance. The Song of Moses uses the same word: "They stirred my jealousy with a not-god / and angered me with their puffs of air" (Deuteronomy 32:21). This site keeps the image here; "worthless idols" gives the sense.

a: for seven days
p: The shortest reign in the Bible. Zimri's name became a byword for a traitor.
b: When King Jehu rode into Jezreel after killing Joram, Jezebel greeted him from her window: "Is it peace, Zimri, who killed his master?" (2 Kings 9:31), mocking him with the name of the man who had killed a king and lasted a week. Zimri is not given a regnal formula with a length in years, only days. In English, John Dryden later used "Zimri" as a name for a fickle schemer in his poem Absalom and Achitophel (1681).

a: all Israel made Omri, the army commander, king over Israel
p: Omri came to power by acclamation of the troops. His origins are unknown; his name may not be Israelite.
b: Kings gives Omri no father's name, which usually means a man of humble or foreign background. Some scholars think the name Omri is Arabic or Amorite rather than Hebrew; others connect it with a Hebrew root meaning "servant" or "sheaf." He was the general in the field, and the army simply proclaimed him king, as Roman legions would later do with their generals.

a: He burned the king's house down over himself
p: Zimri chooses death by fire rather than capture. Ancient kings did the same.
b: The armon was the fortified keep of the palace. Rather than fall into Omri's hands, Zimri set it ablaze with himself inside. Greek writers tell a similar story of the last Assyrian king (Sardanapalus) burning himself in his palace, and the Assyrian king Shamash-shum-ukin of Babylon seems to have died in a burning palace (648 BC). The Bible records few suicides (1 Samuel 31:4–5; 2 Samuel 17:23; Judges 16:30; Matthew 27:5); none is praised.

a: Then the people of Israel split in two
p: After Zimri, the kingdom split between two rivals for about four years.
b: Zimri died in Asa's 27th year (16:15); Omri's sole reign began in Asa's 31st (16:23). The years between seem to be the civil war with Tibni son of Ginath, whom part of the people backed, perhaps the tribes or towns opposed to an army strongman. Omri's twelve years (16:23) probably count from his first proclamation, so they overlap with the war. This is one of the clearest places where Kings' numbers require an overlap of reigns.

a: he named the town he built Samaria, after Shemer, the hill's owner
p: Omri's new capital stood on a hill he bought. Its palace and ivories have been excavated.
b: Samaria (Shomron) is linked here with the name Shemer; it also sounds like shamar, "watch," fitting a hill with views on every side. Harvard excavations (1908–1910) and a joint British expedition led by John Crowfoot (1931–1935) uncovered a royal compound on the summit with fine ashlar masonry, a large palace and hundreds of carved ivory plaques (compare 22:39; Amos 3:15). The city remained Israel's capital until Assyria took it in 722 BC. Buying the land, like David buying Araunah's threshing floor (2 Samuel 24:24), gave Omri a capital owned by his dynasty, free of any tribe's claim. Two talents of silver is about 60–70 kilograms.

a: He did worse than all who were before him
t: Omri in the Bible and in history
p: Kings gives Omri eight verses. Outside records show him as one of Israel's most powerful kings.
b: For Kings, which judges by worship, Omri is simply worse than his predecessors. For historians he founded the strongest dynasty the north ever had. The Mesha Stele (about 840 BC), Moab's royal inscription, says: "Omri was king of Israel, and he oppressed Moab many days," and that Omri took the land of Medeba and Israel lived there "his days and half the days of his son, forty years." Assyrian kings called Israel "the house of Omri" (Bit-Humri) for over a century, and Shalmaneser III's Black Obelisk calls King Jehu "son of Omri" though he had destroyed Omri's dynasty. Ahab, Omri's son, brought 2,000 chariots to the battle of Qarqar in 853 BC. The difference between the two portraits is a good lesson in what Kings is trying to record.

a: His son Ahab became king in his place
t: An extra passage in the Greek
p: After this verse the Greek adds a summary of Jehoshaphat of Judah's reign, a second copy of 22:41–50.
b: Codex Vaticanus has eight extra verses here (16:28a–h) giving the account of Jehoshaphat king of Judah that the Hebrew places at 22:41–50. The Greek also dates Jehoshaphat's accession to Omri's eleventh year rather than Ahab's fourth (22:41). This reflects a different chronology for the kings in the Old Greek tradition, especially in the Lucianic text, which many scholars think may preserve an older system of dates. It is one reason chronologists do not rely on the Hebrew numbers alone. See the variant at 16:29, where the Greek dates Ahab's accession to Jehoshaphat's second year.

a: Jezebel daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians
p: Ethbaal is Ittobaal I of Tyre, a priest-king who seized the throne, according to a Phoenician history quoted by Josephus.
b: Josephus quotes Menander of Ephesus, who drew on the annals of Tyre: Ithobalos (Ittobaal), priest of Astarte, killed the king and reigned thirty-two years (Against Apion 1.123; Antiquities 8.317). "King of the Sidonians" was a common title for the kings of Tyre, who ruled both cities. The marriage sealed an alliance between Israel and Phoenicia, much as Solomon's marriages had. Her name, Hebrew Izevel, may be a play on a Phoenician name, "Where is the Prince (Baal)?"; a seal reading yzbl has been suggested as hers, but that is uncertain. See 18:4 and 21:5–25 for her story.

a: the house of Baal he had built in Samaria
p: Ahab built a temple for Baal in his capital. Jehu later turned it into a latrine.
b: Baal here is probably the Tyrian Baal, Melqart ("king of the city"), or Baal Shamem, "lord of the heavens," the god of Jezebel's homeland; scholars debate which. Building him a temple in the capital made Baal a state god beside the LORD. Jehu gathered Baal's worshipers in this temple, killed them, and made it a latrine "to this day" (2 Kings 10:18–28). No remains of the temple have been identified at Samaria.

a: With Abiram his firstborn he laid its foundation, and with Segub his youngest he set up its gates
p: Joshua's curse on whoever rebuilt Jericho comes true. Did Hiel sacrifice his sons, or did they die?
b: Joshua had said: "Cursed before the LORD be the man who rises up and builds this town again, this Jericho. With his firstborn he will lay its foundation, and with his youngest he will hang its gates" (Joshua 6:26). One view, held by Jewish and Christian commentators since antiquity, is that the sons died as the curse took effect, one at the start and one at the end of the work. Another, common in modern scholarship, is that Hiel sacrificed them as "foundation offerings" to secure the walls, a practice some claim from ancient Near Eastern finds, though the evidence is debated. The verse ends the section on a dark note: under Ahab, old curses are coming true. Jericho seems to have been only lightly settled in this period.
